en: Record of the Meaning of the Scriptural Tradition of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*,
Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Fachong of Qianfu Monastery in the Capital.
I have heard:
The subtle path is profound and remote, its principles transcending both existence and non-existence;
the ultimate Way is ineffable and silent, its form surpassing the reach of sight and hearing.
Yet, as the dark alleys of ignorance accumulate gloom, they rely upon the torch of wisdom to dispel the obscurity;
as the ocean of suffering flows across all, they depend upon the boat of compassion to rescue those drowning.
Thus we know that throughout the three thousandfold world-system, all are moistened by the ferry of outflows, and the hundreds of millions of devas long to emerge from the realm of ignorance.

There was an Emperor named Shan-zhu (Well-Abiding), whose fruition of the Three Refuges was complete and whose causes of the Ten Wholesome Deeds were perfected. He delighted his spirit within the magnificent palace and indulged himself atop the Garden of Precious Flowers;

yet, while he enjoyed wondrous pleasures during the day, the accumulated blessings of a thousand years could not exhaust them, and as he listened to the sounds from the void at night, the remaining calamities of seven days were already imminent.

Having been pressed by the peril of my imminent life, I was suddenly struck with alarm for the body I have received; thus I cast myself upon the Honored One whom I joyfully behold, setting forth the fears born of my distressful hearing. Consequently, I obtained the descent of Hantideva’s thought and the compassionate regard of the Lord of the Imperial Foot, as I looked down upon the precious pond to beg for a means of salvation, and gazed up at the Golden Mountain to entreat him to rescue me.

The World-Honored One, in his great compassion, rescues all beings and propagates the Way to save all living things. Suddenly, a smile appeared upon his vermilion lips, and instantly, light radiated from his deep-blue crown. Thus, he first established the secret methods and sublime principles for extinguishing calamities and eradicating misfortunes, and revealed the auspicious and marvelous prescriptions for prolonging life and increasing longevity. Consequently, Kauśika obtained benefit, hearing the sound of the fourfold eloquence in a single moment;
and Sunakṣatra received grace, uttering three sighs of aspiration over six days.
Dwelling in the precious palace, one praises his virtue and rejoices that his person remains intact;
planting a golden ground to repay his kindness, one further delights in the touching of the crown of the head.
That which is titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī* is the general name for this division, serving as a specific title for this scripture.
As for its literary expression, although the phrasing is concise, the principles are manifold;
as for its practical application, the actual merit is profound and the benefit is great. Why is this so?
When one’s remains are moistened by consecrated earth, the fruits of celestial bliss will surely be attained;
when one’s body brushes away the lingering dust [of transgression], the retributions of hellish suffering shall be severed.
Thus, the pure mani-jewel is fashioned into this exquisite manuscript, and Jambūnada gold is set against these divine verses upon its leaves.
First, when invoking the Buddha’s name, one first sets forth the title of the Hero among Two-Legged Beings;
next, by uttering the word for "Crown," one then describes the noble marks of his singular body.
Because his honor is most exalted, the title is established; thereby, the supreme height of the essence of the teaching is manifested.
"Victorious" (Jiǎngshèng) is named for its ultimate subtlety, signifying the supreme subtlety of the Buddha-mind.
"Dhāraṇī" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Total Retention" (Zǒngchí). It encompasses the profound essence of four meanings and summarizes the ultimate purport of this entire scripture.
"Sūtra" means "constant," and it is also called "turning. The eighty-eight classes of constant sages collectively expound it, hence it is generally termed "constant";
the thirty-three categories of devas together circulate it, hence it is specifically named "turning."
For these reasons, it is titled the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. In order to explain this sūtra, I shall briefly analyze it according to ten sections:
first, explaining its Teacher; second, using the setting to illustrate the events;

third, revealing the intended audience for the teaching; fourth, examining the identity of the manifested bodies; fifth, extracting the essence and substance of the sūtra; sixth, the ritual procedures for hearing the Dharma; seventh, the benefits gained from seeing or hearing [the teaching]; eighth, explaining the title of the sūtra; ninth, the period of its translation; and tenth, the critical analysis and interpretation based on the text.
First, regarding the explanation of the Teacher: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says:
"There are five kinds: first, the speech of the Buddha;
second, the speech of noble disciples; third, the speech of devas; fourth, the speech of ṛṣis; and fifth, the speech of emanations."
"In this present sutra, there are only these four [factors]; as it lacks the discourse of a *ṛṣi* and has been authenticated by the Buddha, it is collectively termed a 'sutra.
This concludes the first explanation regarding the Teacher."
The second [method], expressing the matter by means of location, has three types:
first, expressing the matter by means of a country; second, expressing the matter by means of a grove; and third, expressing the matter by means of a garden.

Furthermore, the first location used to represent the country is Śrāvastī, which in the Han language is called the City of Renown. It is the capital city ruled by King Prasenajit of Central India. It is used to symbolize that the Tathāgata forever transcends the three realms and eternally surpasses the two vehicles; that his compassion moistens the four types of birth and his person is perfected with myriad virtues; therefore, he resides in the City of Far-reaching Renown.

The second, representing the matter of the forest, refers to the Jetavana, which in Chinese is called "Most Victorious Forest. This is the grove bestowed by Prince Jeta, used to symbolize how the Tathāgata’s forest of the seven factors of enlightenment provides compassionate shade for all beings.

Third, as for representing the matter by means of the garden, this refers to the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden; it was a garden bestowed by the elder Sudatta, symbolizing that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable dharmas which he bestows and provides to all impoverished sentient beings.
This concludes the second section, which has finished illustrating the matters by way of their locations.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the teaching according to the capacities of those to be trained: although the gateway of the teaching is one, there are three levels of what is studied. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When the three animals—the hare, the horse, and the elephant—cross a river, there are differences in how deep they perceive it."
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The three sons emerged from the same gate, yet their inclinations were each different.
The Buddha said:
"If I were to teach and transform sentient beings using the Hīnayāna vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed.
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind."

Because the inferior, middling, and superior levels of wisdom each observe distinct objects: through the observation of inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; through the observation of middling wisdom, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and through the observation of superior wisdom, the enlightenment of all Buddhas.
This concludes the third section on how the teachings of the Manifested Vehicle (vyākaraṇa-dharma) accord with the capacities of sentient beings.

Fourth, regarding the similarities and differences in the perceived bodies [of the Buddha]: for example, the Great Brahmā King saw the Buddha’s body as being one thousand feet tall; likewise, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇī saw the Buddha’s body as being sixteen feet tall. He then measured from the crown of the Buddha’s head upward, passing through countless worlds until reaching the Flower-Top (Puṣpadhvaja) Buddha-field, yet upon his return, he still saw the Tathāgata’s body as being sixteen feet tall.
As the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"Non-Buddhists view the Buddha as they would a child; Śrāvakas see only a body sixteen feet tall; Bodhisattvas see the boundless body; and all Buddhas see the Dharma-nature body."
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"For example, as with the pure full moon, which can appear in every body of water; though its reflections are infinite, the original substance remains undifferentiated."
"The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is thus: it manifests various forms according to conditions; though the manifested marks are immeasurable, the essence of the Dharma is without distinction.
This concludes the fourth section on the similarities and differences of the perceived body.

Fifth, regarding the essential body of the sūtras: the non-Buddhists and the various Hīnayāna schools each differ. For instance, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* takes buddha-nature as its essence; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* takes the wisdom of emptiness as its essence; the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* takes the inconceivable as its essence; and the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* takes dhāraṇīs as its essence.

Now, this sutra likewise takes dharanis as its primary theme and all dharmas as the essence of the sutra; therefore, the appendix to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (in four fascicles) quotes the old version of the *Avataṃsaka* to the same effect, saying:
"All worldly realms of the Buddhas can all cause the wheel of Dharma to be turned."
To possess mastery over all phenomena without bondage—this is called the Tathāgata’s true wisdom.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"The substance of the teaching is of two kinds:"
"First, taking the words as the essence of the teaching; second, taking the meaning as the essence of the teaching.
This collectively encompasses everything; now, we take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as the essence of the teaching.
This concludes the fifth section, the presentation of the essential body of the sūtra.
Sixth, regarding the ritual for listening to the Dharma, according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
"The teacher of the Dharma should form three kinds of thoughts:"
First, one should conceive the thought of him as a King of Physicians; second, the thought of him as a Savior from Illness; third, the thought of him as a Remover of Suffering.
The listener of the Dharma should likewise conceive three thoughts:
first, the thought of it as Ambrosia (*amṛta*); second, the thought of it as the Supreme Cream (*sarpirmaṇḍa*); third, the thought of it as the Cure for Disease.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The listener of the Dharma should listen with a single-minded focus and upright gaze, as one who thirsts longs for a drink or as one who hungers longs for food, rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There are three ways of listening to the Dharma:
first, reverently making offerings; second, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it; and third, focusing the mind on it through contemplation."

The first type of reverent offering is virtuous action of the body; it can give rise to the wisdom born of hearing and attain three kinds of merit: first, a long life endowed with the marks of a great man; second, great wealth and abundance of treasures; and third, rebirth through transformation within a lotus flower.

Second, as for upholding, reciting, and chanting, this is a wholesome action of speech that can give rise to wisdom born of reflection and yields four kinds of merit: first, what one says is trusted by others; second, what one says is followed by others; third, one’s family and retinue remain harmonious and complete; and fourth, one is not subjected to slander.

Third, as for the cultivation of mindfulness and reflection, this is wholesome mental action that can generate wisdom born of cultivation and attain three kinds of merit: first, clothing and food appear spontaneously; second, one attains great physical beauty; and third, one attains great wisdom.
This concludes the sixth procedure for listening to the Dharma.
Regarding the seventh point, the benefits gained through seeing and hearing, there are two types:
first, gaining benefit through seeing and hearing; second, not gaining benefit because one neither sees nor hears.
First, regarding those who gain benefit through seeing and hearing, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who hear even once a Mahāyāna sūtra, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas they shall not fall into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one plants roots of goodness before as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, one will be able to hear the Mahāyāna sūtras for a time.
If one plants roots of goodness before as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in two Ganges Rivers, one will be able to hear the Mahāyāna sūtras and will not give rise to slander."
Having planted roots of goodness before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of three Ganges Rivers, one is able to joyfully prostrate;
having planted roots of goodness before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of four Ganges Rivers, one is able to transcribe and circulate [the teachings].
"Having planted roots of goodness before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers, one will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra].
It is clearly understood that Mahāyāna sūtras are extremely difficult to encounter, and so forth.
Furthermore, the latter part of this sutra states:

"If anyone should hear this dhāraṇī for even a brief moment, all evil karma accumulated over a thousand kalpas will be completely eradicated upon hearing it; they shall no longer receive a body in the evil realms and will be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Suppose there were a person who opened the royal treasury and practiced giving for a single day; the merit obtained would be immeasurable and boundless, yet it would not equal that of a person who recites the Buddha’s name even once. How much more so for one who is able to hear the Mahāyāna sūtras."
Furthermore, the *Dīpāyana-sūtra* states:
"Regardless of whether one listens to the Dharma, merely entering a monastery yields five kinds of merit:
first, physical comeliness, because upon seeing the Triple Gem, the mind gives rise to joy."
Second is a pleasant voice, for the sake of mindfulness of the Buddha;
third is rebirth in heaven, because of the absence of other evil karma;
fourth is nobility, for the sake of paying homage to all the Triple Gem.
Fifth, they attain the realization of nirvana because they possess residual merit.
Regarding the second case—those who neither see, nor hear, nor obtain benefit—there are seven types:

first, sentient beings who commit evil; second, sentient beings experiencing pleasure; third, sentient beings in the hells; fourth, sentient beings as hungry ghosts; fifth, sentient beings as animals; sixth, sentient beings afflicted by illness; and seventh, sentient beings traveling afar.
The first type of sentient beings who commit evil are those who, out of greed, commit the ten non-virtuous actions and the five heinous crimes; they shall not hear this sutra, and so forth.

The second type of sentient beings who experience pleasure are those such as the wealthy and noble among humans, who wear fine silks and brocades and consume wine and meat; or those in the various heavens of the upper realms who, clad in robes of three *zhu* weight, indulge in the pleasures of the five desires and receive great joy; they shall not hear this sutra, and so forth.

As for the sentient beings in the third hell, throughout the eight hells, the four annexes, and the sixteen compartments, there are mountains of knives filling their view, sword-trees piercing their bodies, fierce fires burning above, and blades of wheels cutting below; because they greedily endure such suffering, they are unable to hear the sutras, and so forth.
The fourth is hungry ghosts, the fifth is animals, the sixth is illness, and the seventh is long-distance travel; these four types are explained according to their respective meanings, and so forth.
The eighth section explains the title of the sūtra, which has three aspects:
first, it is named the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-dhāraṇī*; second, it is named "Extending Life"; and third, it is named "Excellence and Auspiciousness."
"Buddha" is the title for one who has attained the three types of awakening; therefore, he is called Buddha.
"Crown" (uṣṇīṣa) refers to the most preeminent part of the body, established as the "crown.
"Venerable" (bhadanta) means that he is honored by all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. "Victorious" (jina) means that he cannot be surpassed by those of the two vehicles.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). There are four meanings of total retention, as fully explained above; therefore, it is called the *Buddhoṣṇīṣavijayadhāraṇīsūtra*.

Ninth, regarding the time and circumstances of the translation: In the southwestern region known as Jibin, there was a Brahmin named Buddhapāli. Having been born during the Age of Dharma-Decline (mofa), he had not beheld the countenance of a Buddha. He perused all available books and examined the sūtras and śāstras, until he heard that the Great Being Mañjuśrī resided at Mount Wutai, expounding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the sake of various bodhisattvas. Thereupon, taking his mendicant’s staff with him and carrying his robes and bowl upon his person, he set out from India and traveled to China.

In the first year of the Yifeng era, he arrived at the foot of Mount Wutai. There, black clouds gathered heavily and white mists spread vast and thick; the path by which they came was unknown, and the way they departed could not be discerned. He then prostrated himself with utmost sincerity, taking refuge with his five limbs touching the ground. In an instant, the clouds parted and the mists dispersed, clearing away everything so that not a trace of smoke or cloud remained.

Proceeding further for several dozen li, he beheld high mountains rising from the earth and emerald ridges reaching toward the heavens. With a reverent spirit and resolute will, he ascended slowly and steadily; after traveling five li, he suddenly saw auspicious clouds like a canopy.

He wept even more bitterly, his tears flowing freely, and with palms joined, he sighed: "I am but an ordinary man, while the Sage is a Great Sage. Were it not for the hidden grace of the divine, how could I have obtained this vision?"

Before he had even raised his head, he suddenly saw an old man dressed in plain white garments with snow-white hair, whose dignified bearing was solemn and majestic. Speaking in the accent of a Brahmin, the man said to Buddhatāpali, "Virtuous One, you have come from afar;
you must have endured great hardship."
Pāli said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to Mañjuśrī; how could I decline such hardship?
The old man said:

“In this land, sentient beings who commit transgressions are many, while those who cultivate merit are few; those who fall into the hells after death are immeasurable and boundless, whereas those born in the various pure lands are not even one in ten thousand.”
"That *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī* provides great salvation for the sentient beings of this land; I do not know whether the Venerable One has brought the scripture with you.
Buddhapālita replied, "I have not brought even a single scripture or treatise; I have come here solely for the purpose of paying homage to Mañjuśrī."
The old man said, "Virtuous One!

You should return to the Western Land to fetch this sutra and extensively benefit all beings, opening the gates of heaven and delivering those suffering in hell. When we meet again in the future, I shall certainly show you Mañjuśrī; even if you were to see him now, you might not necessarily recognize him."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

At that time, Buddhapālita was as if mourning the loss of a close kinsman; weeping and filled with grief and distress, he then took up his staff and traveled westward. Enduring repeated cycles of cold and heat, he journeyed ninety thousand *li*, coming and going for more than ten years.

In the second year of the Yongchun era, he returned to the Great Tang; the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought were presented to the imperial palace, along with a detailed account of the circumstances regarding the elderly man, submitted all at once.

This month, I was graced by repeated inquiries and treated with exceptional courtesy as a distinguished guest; consequently, an edict was issued through the Right Office granting me thirty bolts of silk.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master from Central India, Divākara—translated into Chinese as Rìzhào (Sunlight)—had spread the wind of the Dharma throughout the Five Indias and circulated its transformation across the Nine Provinces. By imperial decree, this Dharma Master was invited, and Du Xingyi, Director of the Court of State Ceremonials, and others were summoned to perform the translations within the palace. Once these writings were completed, they were presented to His Majesty.

Having never heard such teachings before, he revered them with redoubled sincerity; each day he would first recite them several times before attending to the myriad affairs of state, keeping them secret within the inner palace so that they did not reach the outside world.
Poli reflected privately, saying:

"This divine person has responded to our needs and fully described the sublime efficacy [of this teaching]. If the sentient beings of this land are to receive its nourishment, how could the Emperor alone rely upon it, while the myriad subjects are left without support?"

"Recently, we have entrusted our lives to this cause and cast aside our own existence, not shrinking from toil and hardship, in the hope that gods and humans may receive blessings and that both the hidden and the manifest realms may find peace.

Thereupon, he presented his petition to the Purple Microcosm (the Emperor), hoping for profound grace to flow forth; he then disseminated the texts of the scriptures to instruct those who had not yet heard them.
The Emperor, moved by this sincere devotion, granted his former wish, decreeing that those [texts] not yet transmitted be appended and those already translated be preserved.

Having thus fulfilled his original aspiration, he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; he received them with bowed head and prostrations, his reverence exceeding his usual constancy a hundredfold.
However, as the script upon the palm leaves had not yet had its phrases and meanings resolved, how could it be taught to future generations without a re-translation?

The śramaṇa Shunzheng, a monk of Ximing Monastery, was exquisitely proficient in Sanskrit and possessed a profound understanding of the scriptural texts. He, together with the Venerable Cefashi and the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, re-translated [the text] at Ximing Monastery. This was done because although the earlier translation by Tripiṭaka Master Rizi and the subsequent translation by Dharma Master Boli differed slightly in style—being respectively more refined and more vernacular—their underlying principles were no different. Examining these two versions, they were both translations made in the second year of the Yongchun era.

Boli returned carrying the Sanskrit manuscript to Mount Wutai; from that time until the present, no further news of him has been heard. Thus we know that this refers to the great skillful means of Mañjuśrī in guiding and receiving others—one who appears but once in a thousand years.
There is also one version of the old translation by Kumārajīva.
The tenth [section] provides an interpretation based on the text.
"Thus" means:
The commentary states:
This scripture consists of one volume, which is divided into three parts. First, the three parts are explained; subsequently, the two introductory sections are explained.
Regarding the three parts: first, the Part on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching.
2. The section on what is taught in the holy scriptures;
3. The section on practicing in accordance with the teachings.
From the sūtra’s "Thus have I heard" down to "as fully explained above," this constitutes the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching.
From "At that time, the Tathāgata" down to "all came to see me" is the section on the teaching as proclaimed by the Sage.
From "At that time, the Lord of Devas" down to "faithfully accepting and practicing" is the section on practicing in accordance with the teaching.

Now, when the Sage expounds the Dharma, he must necessarily provide an introduction; those to be transformed among the common masses require a sense of wonder to be stirred. If he were to speak abruptly, they would fail to give rise to feelings of reverence; therefore, the Sūtra first sets forth the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching.
Having purified one’s mind and established faith, one then opens the school and receives the Dharma; next is the section clarifying what is taught in the sacred teachings.

Because great compassion for all sentient beings is boundless and they have not yet attained tranquility, these instructions were transmitted; hence, this is called the section on "Receiving and Practicing According to the Teachings."
Within the first section, "The Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching," there are further two divisions:
first, the *Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna* (Sequence of Testimony and Faith); second, the *Prastāvanā-nidāna* (Sequence of the Arousing).
From "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) down to "together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bodhisattvas," is the Sequence of Testimony and Faith.
From "At that time, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" down to "as fully described above," this constitutes the Prologue of the Occasion (Nidāna).
First, the Prologue of Testimony (Śraddhā-viniścaya) was explained; subsequently, the Prologue of the Occasion is explained.

Regarding the "Prologue of Certification and Faith," there are six phrases of sūtra text: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly.
If the six meanings are complete, one is able to realize and believe them; if the six meanings are insufficient, they cannot be established as proof.
Thus, the verse of Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
"The first three clarify the disciples, and the latter three establish the Teacher’s teaching; all sūtras and dharma-gates are like this."
Within the accomplishment of faith, it is further divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the origin of existence;
second, clarifying the six accomplishments.
Third, correctly explaining his faith. First, to clarify the origins of its existence:

on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu of Zhou, the year of Renshen, at dawn, a black wind suddenly arose in a violent gale. The sun lost its brilliance, houses were blown down, trees were broken, and the earth shook violently. After passing through the state of Qi, the world fell into great darkness. From the west, twelve rays of white light emerged, penetrating through from left to right.
King Mu asked the Grand Historian Hu Du: "What kind of omen is this?"
Ghṛtapada replied, "In the western direction there is a Great Sage who is about to enter parinirvāṇa; therefore, he manifests this sign.

At that time, it was the day when the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was about to enter nirvana. Seeing the Buddha about to enter nirvana, Ānanda’s heart was filled with grief and distress, and he wept with flowing tears as if he had lost his own parents.
Then the Elder Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"How could he be like an ordinary person who possesses grief and affliction? You should ask the Tathāgata about four great matters."
This is the reason for the existence of the "first bhava.
Second, regarding the manifestation of the six accomplishments, there are three aspects:
first, to sever doubt;
Second, to give rise to faith;
third, to stop slander.
Regarding the first, the severing of doubt, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees on the fifteenth day of the second month, the devas feared that the Dharma would perish. They went to Kāśyapa, prostrated themselves before Mahākāśyapa, and spoke this verse:

'In old age, desire, anger, and pride have been eliminated; His form is like a pillar of purple-gold. From top to bottom, his majesty is wondrous and peerless; His eyes are clear and pure like a lotus flower. "
At that time, after the devas had finished praising him with verses, they addressed Kāśyapa, saying:

"Virtuous One! The ship of the Dharma is about to sink; the city of the Dharma is about to collapse; the ocean of the Dharma is about to dry up; the banner of the Dharma is about to fall; and the lamp of the Dharma is about to be extinguished."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa replied to the devas, saying, "The world is impermanent;
before long it will fall into blindness and darkness.
He then silently accepted their invitation.
At that time, the devas and others, having paid homage to Kāśyapa, each returned to their own celestial palaces.
Then Mahākāśyapa reflected to himself:
"In order that I may repay the Buddha's kindness, I shall compile the treasury of the Dharma for the sake of all devas and humans."
Thereupon, he ascended into the air and stood atop Mount Sumeru; striking the great bell and the wooden mallet, he spoke these verses:
"O disciples of the Buddha!
If you would keep the Buddha in mind, you should repay the Buddha's kindness and not enter into nirvana."
When the sound of this ghaṇṭā and the words of Kāśyapa are transmitted, they will simultaneously pervade the trichiliocosm; all disciples of the Buddha shall be able to hear my words.
Those who had attained arhatship gathered together at once at the abode of Mahākāśyapa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The Buddha is about to pass into extinction, and now the Dharma is likewise about to perish. We should convene a council; once the council is concluded, we shall follow him into nirvana."

At that time, Mahākāśyapa arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and selected one thousand people; with the sole exception of Ānanda, who had not yet attained arhatship, the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine were all arhats.
Question:
"Why did you take exactly one thousand people, neither more nor less? Answer:
"King Bimbisāra was the father of King Ajātaśatru;
he made a vow to provide offerings to a thousand monks every day, and his son, King Ajātaśatru, likewise followed his father's practice."
When Mahākāśyapa had arrived at Rājagṛha, he addressed King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"I now wish to compile the Dharma-piṭaka; may Your Majesty provide the necessary offerings."
At that time, Kāśyapa, together with one thousand people, went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to observe the summer retreat for three months.

When the recitation of the precepts was completed on the first day of the fifteenth day, Mahākāśyapa immediately entered meditative concentration to observe among the assembly who possessed afflictions and should be expelled; he found that there was only Ānanda, while all the others were Arhats.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa took Ānanda by the hand and led him out from the assembly, saying to him:
"This is a pure assembly compiling the Tripiṭaka; as your fetters are not yet exhausted, you should not remain here."
At that time, Ānanda felt ashamed and thought to himself:

"I have served the World-Honored One for twenty-five years, yet never before have I experienced such arising of suffering and distress; this is truly the result of his great compassion and forbearance."
He said to Kāśyapa,
"I have left behind these remaining fetters for the sake of making offerings.
Kāśyapa said:
"You further have six types of *duṣkṛta* offenses that must be confessed:
first, you requested that women be ordained, which will shorten the duration of my True Dharma by five hundred years;
second, you did not request the Buddha to remain [in this world]."
Third, not offering water to the Buddha;
fourth, folding the *uttarāsaṅga* robe and using it as a pillow while lying down;
fifth, treading upon the *saṃghāṭī* robe of the Buddha.
"Sixth, you gazed upon women with the Buddha’s private organ [the *kośagatavastiguhya*].
Having committed these six offenses, you should repent.
Ānanda replied:
"I have heard that the Buddhas of the past and future worlds all possess four [great powers], which is why I requested that women be permitted to leave the household life.
As for my not having requested that the Buddha remain in the world, it was because my mind was obscured by Māra."
Regarding the third reason for not offering water to the Buddha: five hundred chariots had passed through the upstream area, rendering the water turbid and unfit to be offered to the Buddha.
The fourth [rule] regarding folding the *uttarāsaṅga* before lying down is for the sake of preventing bodily pain.
The fifth rule regarding folding the Buddha’s *saṃghāṭī* robe and stepping upon it with one's feet is for the sake of preventing the wind from blowing it askew so that it slips beneath the feet.
"Sixth, as for displaying the Buddha’s private organ to women, it was intended to cause women to feel revulsion.

Ānanda immediately removed his leather sandals in the midst of the assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and confessed his *duṣkṛta* offense. Once the confession was completed, Mahākāśyapa led Ānanda out from the midst of the Saṃgha by the hand and addressed him, saying:
"If your residual fetters are not yet exhausted, do not come here again."
Thereupon they closed the door and addressed one another, saying,
"Who among us is capable of compiling the Vinaya Piṭaka?
At that time, Aniruddha spoke:
“Śāriputra’s disciple Kapphiṇa is well-versed in the Vinaya; he is currently in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, in the Śirīṣa Garden, preaching the Vinaya.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa dispatched an arhat to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven on a mission for the Saṃgha. Like a swift-flying goose, he traveled to the heavens and went to where Kapphiṇa was. He prostrated himself at his feet, inquired after his well-being, and said:
“Venerable One!...”
"In Jambudvīpa there is currently a matter concerning the Saṃgha;
you should go there with all haste. Kauṇḍinya asked, "Is there no dispute within the Saṃgha?"
"Has the Buddha-Sun entered parinirvāṇa?
Has the Saṃgha been split?
The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Kauṇḍinya said, "The Buddha has passed away too soon;
the Eye of the World has been extinguished."
He asked again,
"Is my preceptor Śāriputra here?
He replied:
"He has already entered nirvana.
He asked again,
"Is Mahāmaudgalyāyana there?"
He replied,
"They too have entered nirvāṇa.
At that time, Kavaṇḍaka addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Now that I have lost my Great Teacher who has transcended desire, and my Upādhyāya has also passed away, what further purpose is there for me to go elsewhere?
I cannot descend again to Jambudvīpa; I shall enter Parinirvāṇa right here."

Having spoken these words, he immediately entered meditative concentration and leaped up into the air, manifesting the eighteen transformations. Having displayed these supernatural feats, he emanated from his own heart a fire that consumed his body; from within the flames, water emerged and divided into four streams, flowing down to the place where Mahākāśyapa was compiling the Tripiṭaka.

Amidst the water, a voice spoke this verse: "Kauṇḍinya bows his head in homage to the Great Virtuous Saṃgha, the foremost among all assemblies. Hearing that the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, I follow him, just as when a great elephant departs, the young elephant follows."

At that time, the junior bhikṣu returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Jambudvīpa, the place where the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, to manifest Ānanda’s fruition. At that moment, Ānanda was about to realize arhatship; he immediately knocked on the hall door, and Mahākāśyapa asked, “Who is knocking at the door?”
Ānanda replied, "I am Ānanda. Kāśyapa asked:
"Why have you come?
Ānanda replied once more,
"I have already realized arhatship."
Kāśyapa replied, "Since you have realized arhatship, enter as you please.

Once Ānanda had entered, Kāśyapa directed him to ascend the high seat. After he had ascended the seat, [he described] how the Tathāgata was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. At that time, Ānanda, with single-minded devotion and palms joined, faced the place where the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and spoke this verse:

"When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, I was not present at that time; I heard it through successive reports that the Buddha was in Vārāṇasī, where he opened the gate of ambrosia for the five bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained the vision of the Path, as did eighty thousand devas who heard this and likewise attained the vision of the Path."
When Ānanda had spoken this verse, the thousand arhats all said, "The power of impermanence is great;
we have seen the Buddha with our own eyes.
In unison, they spoke this verse:

"I behold the physical marks of the Buddha's body, like a mountain of purple gold; yet these wondrous marks and manifold virtues have ceased, and only the name remains. Therefore, you should employ skillful means to emerge from the triple world; diligently accumulate all roots of goodness, for Nirvana is the supreme bliss."
After these one thousand arhats had spoken this verse, they returned to their original seats.

Then Mahākāśyapa, in the presence of Upāli, first compiled the five divisions of the Vinaya Piṭaka; next, in the presence of Ānanda, he compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka and the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Furthermore, based on the faithful accounts from the Tathāgata’s first turning of the Wheel of Dharma until his parinirvāṇa, he compiled the four Āgamas:
first, the Ekottarika Āgama; [and so forth].
2. Dīrgha Āgama; 3. Madhyama Āgama; 4. Saṃyukta Āgama.
These are collectively termed the Sūtra Piṭaka.
At that time, after Mahākāśyapa had completed the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka, he addressed his disciples on Vulture Peak Mountain, saying:
"This afternoon, at the hour of *pradoṣa*, shall be the time of my entry into *nirvāṇa*."
The disciples all descended the mountain at once and informed all the nobles of Rājagṛha, saying:
"Mahākāśyapa entered nirvāṇa this very day at the hour of late afternoon."

At that time, all the people, each harboring grief and distress, went together to where Mahākāśyapa was. Kāśyapa preached various essential teachings for them; he then donned the *saṃghāṭī* robe belonging to the Buddha, took up his bowl and robes, and held a *khakkhara* staff in his hand. Like a golden-winged garuḍa leaping into the air, he manifested the eighteen transformations.
Having displayed these supernatural powers, he made this vow: "May this body of mine behold Maitreya."

Having finished making this vow, he entered directly into Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as if entering soft mud; once inside, the mountain closed back up again. He remained there waiting for Maitreya. When the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years and the height of a person is eighty feet, Maitreya Buddha will appear in the world, with a height of one hundred and sixty feet, a face twenty-four feet wide, and a halo extending ten *li*. He will deliver the Dharma in three assemblies to save sentient beings.

When the people were indolent, Maitreya Buddha then pressed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with his toe, causing the mountain to open. Once it had opened, Mahākāśyapa donned his saṃghāṭī robe and went forth to pay homage to Maitreya; he ascended into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations. Having displayed these miraculous powers, he entered nirvāṇa, at which time he delivered countless beings.
This constitutes the first elimination of doubt.

Regarding the second, the generation of faith: just as the great earth can produce grasses and trees, and just as parents can nourish and sustain their children, so too does the Buddha Jewel nurture and grow the Dharma-body.
This constitutes the second stage, the arising of faith.
Non-Buddhist scriptures lack these six meanings, which is why they are subject to censure.

The third stage is the correct understanding of that faith; "thus" (evam) signifies that the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously realized, principle and phenomena are presented together, teacher and disciple are equally honored, and ordinary beings and sages alike find their way home. Even those on the ten stages can only gaze at it from afar, and those of the three vehicles do not know its source.
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* states:
"Such [phenomena] are auspicious omens of response and resonance.
Therefore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:"
"Whenever the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he first manifests three kinds of great and auspicious omens:
first, the Brahma-voice; second, wondrous fragrance; and third, radiant light."
These three kinds of manifestations now transform into jeweled terraces that extend throughout the ten directions, causing the entire world-system to tremble universally.

Sentient beings who behold them have the hairs on their bodies stand on end and give rise to superior states of mind; they are able to cause the afflictions of sentient beings to crumble away, just as when the *viśvabheṣaja* medicine is placed among poisonous drugs, causing those poisons to transform into nectar (*amṛta*). In this same way, the auspicious and wondrous medicine is placed within the eighty-four thousand defilements, transforming them into the nectar of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Such auspicious omens as these can be briefly explained through ten metaphors: first, the metaphor of the accumulated firewood;

second, the metaphor of the lion’s sinew; third, the metaphor of the wheel-turning king; fourth, the metaphor of the essence of jewels; fifth, the metaphor of sandalwood; sixth, the metaphor of piṅgala; seventh, the metaphor of Jīvaka’s drum; eighth, the metaphor of lion’s milk; ninth, the metaphor of the vessel of merit; and tenth, the metaphor of the crystal bead."
First, he burned [the city] by piling up firewood;
second, he used a lion’s sinew as a lute string;
third, he subdued [the enemy] with a wheel.
4. The *Ratnaraśmi* (*寶精諭光明*).
5. The *Candana* (*檀香諭者*), which encompasses a square area of forty *li* around an *elā* forest.
6. The *Piṅgala* (*賓伽羅諭者*); as stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*:

"In the kingdom of Kaliṅga there is a treasure-store of the seven jewels called Piṅgala, which is replete with the seven precious gems; sentient beings may take from it without it ever being exhausted.
Faith is also like this, for it can give rise to all the Dharma-jewels of the Buddhas.
Seventh is the analogy of Jīvaka and the drum. As stated in the *Vyākhyāyukti*: "Regarding Jīvaka’s drum:

whenever all sentient beings have entered into battle and are struck by various poisoned arrows, if he strikes the drum once, all the poisoned arrows will emerge simultaneously, and they will be free from all pain."
Faith is also like this: once the mind of faith is aroused, it can cause the arrows of the three poisons to be extracted all at once.
Eighth is the parable of the lion’s milk: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, “Just as when lion’s milk is poured into other milks, they are all transformed into water.”
Faith is also like this: it can transform all afflictions into the water of the Dharma and the profound clarity of Bodhi.
Ninth, the analogy of the Vase of Merit: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There was a Brahmin who served the Goddess of Merit for twelve years, seeking to have his wishes fulfilled."
When twelve years had passed, Puṇyavatī appeared and presented him with a flask, saying:
"Whatever you require, seek from this flask and it shall be obtained according to your wish."
Faith is also like this; it can give rise to all virtuous merits and qualities.
Tenth, the analogy of the crystal:
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states, "When there is turbid water, by the power of placing this jewel within it, the water immediately becomes clear and pure."
Faith is also like this: it can cause all the turbidity of lack of faith to become completely pure.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"That which is 'thus' (evam) is called 'thus' because it is free from all forms of slander."
There are five kinds of slander:
first, slander by way of exaggeration;
second, slander by way of depreciation.
3. Denial through contradiction;
4. denial through delusion;
5. denial through frivolous proliferation.
To say that the causes and effects in this sutra definitely and truly exist is the slander of superimposition;
to say that the causes and effects in this sutra truly do not exist is the slander of denial;
to say that the causes and effects in this sutra both exist and do not exist is the slander of contradiction.
To say that the cause and effect of this sutra are neither existent nor non-existent is the slander of ignorance;
to say that the cause and effect of this sutra are neither non-existent nor non-non-existent is the slander of frivolous conceptualization.
It is called "thus" (*tathā*) because it is free from the five types of false accusation.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"'Thus' is explained based on four meanings:"
First, the explanation by way of analogy;
second, the explanation by way of instruction;
third, the explanation by way of question and answer.
Fourth is the explanation by way of permission.
First, the explanation by way of analogy: "Your merit and nobility now are like those of Vaiśravaṇa.
Second, the explanation by way of instruction: "You should recite and study in this manner, and practice in this manner."
The third, the explanation by way of question and answer, is: "Thus have I heard; thus it was proclaimed.
The fourth, the explanation by way of granting permission, is: "I shall proclaim it for you in this manner."
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty said:
"Such words as these were spoken by the Buddha; therefore, one says 'Thus' (evam).
Furthermore, Dharma Master Jingtai said:
"‘Thus’ (evam) refers directly to the Dharma; it is a term of certainty. Since everything that is taught according to the Dharma is true, one says ‘thus.
Furthermore, Master Zhao explained:

‘Faith is the accord with the principle of what is spoken; accord is the fulfillment of the way between teacher and disciple. Therefore, at the beginning of the sutra, one establishes the statement “thus.”'"
Now, the explanation is as follows:

"Thus" (evam) refers to that which accords with the words of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; "is" (iti) refers to that which has been spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time; therefore, it is called "thus" (evam).
Furthermore, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) from the Liang dynasty states:
"There are three kinds of faith:
first, faith in actual existence;..."
Second, one believes that it can be attained;
third, one believes that there are infinite merits.
For example, just as fire-nature certainly exists within wood and is obtained by drilling, and once obtained, various functions are realized, so too is the Buddha-nature.
Now, I shall briefly provide ten explanations:
First, it is the initial cause for entering the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), and the gradual fruition of escaping the cage of ordinary beings.
Second, it is the sublime beginning of partaking in the flavor of the Dharma, and the bearing of the Dharma-treasure upon both shoulders.
Third, it is the primary source for acquiring the seven riches and the initial aspiration for attaining the power of a king.
Fourth, it is that upon which the three vehicles rely, and by means of which the myriad practices are cultivated.
Fifth, it is a clear pearl for the waters of the tranquil mind, illuminating the turbidity of the nature of consciousness.
Sixth, it emerges from the midst of the mud.
Seventh, it transcends the perilous path of birth and death.
8. A vessel for crossing the sea of suffering;
9. Hands and feet for gathering the jewels of the Dharma;
10. Armor for roaming through the wilderness.
Therefore, within the eleven wholesome [mental factors] of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are three sections:
first, the basis for their existence; second, the explanation of faith among the six [root virtues]; and third, [the explanation of the remaining factors].
Third, severing doubt and engendering faith to cease slander, taking pure faith as its essence; it is like a crystal bead that can clarify turbid water.
Although there have been three different types mentioned above, this concludes the general explanation of the first [stage], the accomplishment of faith.
Regarding "I who have heard":
the commentary states that this refers to the accomplishment of the second hearing.
It is also analyzed according to three gates:
first, the explanation of Ānanda’s name;
second, the explanation of Ānanda’s causes.
Third, the correct explanation of the character *wen* (hearing).
First, regarding Ānanda’s etymology: this is a Sanskrit term; in Chinese it is translated as "Joyful" (*huānxǐ*). Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"King Siṃhahanu had four sons, all of whom became kings."
First, named Śuddhodana;
second, named Śuklodana;
third, named Droṇodana.
Fourth, he was named Amṛtodana.
Furthermore, King Śuddhodana had two sons:
the first was named Siddhārtha, and the second was named Nanda.
King Śuklodana also had two sons:
the first was named Bhadrika, and the second was named Tiṣya.
King Droṇodana also had two sons:
The first was named Devadatta, and the second was named Ānanda.
King Amṛtodana also had two sons:
the first was named Mahānāman, and the second was named Aniruddha.

As for the Crown Prince Siddhārtha of the Pure Brahmā King, at the age of nineteen he renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch. On the eighth day of the second month, at midnight during the hour of the rat, he leaped over the city walls to leave the household life. With single-minded resolve, he sat in peaceful dhyāna with palms joined and a concentrated mind; he practiced austerities for six years, consuming only hemp and wheat daily until his skin and bones were joined together.
When the King heard this, he wept bitterly and sighed, saying: "My son has abandoned the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch, yet he returns empty-handed with nothing gained."
After the Bodhisattva had finished consuming the fragrant milk, he entered the Nairañjanā River to wash his body; having done so, he went to the Vajrāsana and made this vow:
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained perfect enlightenment."
After these words were spoken, heaven and earth shook and the palace of Māra was thrown into turmoil.

At that time, seeing that the Bodhisattva was about to attain enlightenment, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān led eighty billion demonesses and ghosts, filling an area of sixty yojanas with various forms of harassment, coming to terrify the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi of the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), causing the swords and arrows of Māra to be transformed into lotus flowers.
Realizing he was no match, Māra went immediately to King Śuddhodana’s palace to distress his father, the king, proclaiming from the midst of the sky:
"Your son passed away last night."
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with terror and unconsciously fell from his bed; after a long while he regained consciousness, and weeping with streaming tears, he spoke these verses:
"The words of Āyita were false, and the auspicious signs bore no fruit; though I first attained the name of 'Prosperity,' I have gained nothing at all."

When King Śuddhodana had spoken these words, the Bodhi-tree deity, seeing that the Buddha had attained enlightenment, took celestial māndārava flowers and went to King Śuddhodana’s palace, speaking this verse from mid-air:
“Your son has already attained the Way; The hosts of Māra have been defeated and dispersed. His radiance is like the sun and moon, Universally illuminating the lands of the ten directions.”
At that time, the king said with doubt:
"Previously you said my son was already dead, yet now you say he has attained Buddhahood; what do these words mean?
The tree deity replied:
"The one before you was the Māra King who came to trouble you; I am a tree deity of the Bodhi tree, come now to congratulate you.
The King then said joyfully, "My son has renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning King to become a Dharma-Wheel Turning King; there is no loss for either side."
While King Śuddhodana was in the midst of his great joy, King Droṇodana came to inform King Śuddhodana, saying:
"The consort of my noble younger brother has given birth to a son."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and said:
"All manner of celebrations have come together; because of this happiness, let it be named 'Joyful' (Nandana).
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses. The great ocean waters of the Buddha-Dharma flow into the heart of Ānanda.
This concludes the first explanation of the name Ānanda.
The second explanation concerns the causes for Ānanda’s [attainment]. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"I and Ānanda simultaneously resolved our minds toward enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja; I constantly practiced diligence, while Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning."

Furthermore, when Śākyamuni Buddha was a śrāmaṇera under Kāśyapa Buddha in the past, his preceptor required him to recite a thousand words every day and also commanded him to constantly beg for food for two people. Fearing that he would not be able to master the sutras, the boy wept along the way.
At that time, there was an elder who asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Why are you so distressed?
The śrāmaṇera replied:

"My preceptor has ordered me to recite a thousand words and further commanded me to constantly beg for food for two people; I fear I shall not be able to master the sutra, which is why I am distressed."
The elder replied, "You may recite the sutras with a peaceful mind;

from this day forward, come regularly to my household as a disciple to receive food for two people. If you attain Buddhahood, I pray that you will accept me as a disciple within your Dharma-treasury."
The novice who recited the sūtras in the past was Śākyamuni Buddha, and the elder who gave him food was Ānanda.
This concludes the second explanation of the causes regarding Ānanda.
Third, the correct explanation of the text: The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"I" refers to the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) for the aggregates (*skandha*). "Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*) giving rise to consciousness to listen to and receive what is spoken. Setting aside the particulars and adopting the general, it is therefore said, "I heard."
Question: "The Buddha praised non-self; why then do the Bodhisattvas who transmit the Dharma say, 'Thus have I heard'? Answer:
"This Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma always relies upon two truths: first, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and second, ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
To say 'I heard' is merely a statement according to conventional truth."
The Buddha said: "The various faculties are spoken of as 'self' or 'non-self,' yet within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.
Furthermore, Master Lang explained:
"The faculties cannot hear, and the ear-consciousness cannot know; even when combined they cannot hear—this is what is meant by 'not hearing.'"
Having personally received the oral instructions and selected from among various interpretations and transmissions, it is said: "Thus have I heard.
A question is raised:

"The Tathāgata preached the Dharma for fifty years, yet Ānanda had served the Buddha for only twenty-five of those years. During the first twenty-five years, Ānanda did not hear anything at all; why then is the entire teaching of this era attributed to 'Thus have I heard'?"
He replied:
"According to the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), it states:
'For Ānanda’s sake, [the Buddha] repeated the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Therefore, the teachings of this entire dispensation all begin with the words, 'Thus have I heard.'"
Question: "Why is it that Ānanda is able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures? Answer:
“Ānanda attained the Suvarṇapuṣpa Samādhi and was able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
‘Ānanda is fully endowed with eight qualities and is able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures.’”

First, the faculty of faith is firm and solid; second, the mind is upright and sincere; third, the body is free from suffering and pain; fourth, one is constantly diligent and energetic; fifth, one is fully endowed with mindfulness; sixth, the mind is free from arrogance; seventh, one achieves the wisdom born of hearing; eighth, wisdom arises from what has been heard.

"Endowed with the eight qualities, one is able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures. With a face like the full moon, men and women rush toward him; with eyes like blue lotuses, noble and humble alike look up to him. At night, the Buddha’s light shines forth as he hears the joyful proclamations; at dawn, the celestial blossoms open as he returns to the dance of joy. The Tathāgata, in expounding the Dharma, possesses the capacity to receive [the truth] as it flows from the vase; the Great Sage, in propagating the sutras, possesses the beauty of golden words. Hearing once, they all comprehend; practicing together the eight qualities, this is why those of the four modes of birth hear it again, and why throughout the ten directions it is chanted anew. Having personally received the sounds and meanings, and being distinguished from collateral transmissions, it is therefore said: "Thus have I heard."
Although there have been three different versions above, this concludes the general explanation of the second [topic], the accomplishment of hearing.
Regarding "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*):
the commentary states:
This is the accomplishment of the third period.
It is also analyzed through three gates:
first, the explanation of the provisional name of the period;
The second [section] explains the time of the inconceivable;
the third provides the formal explanation of that time.
Regarding the first, the time of conventional designation, it is like the momentum of a potter’s wheel at its peak.
Furthermore, as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The shortest unit of time is one *kṣaṇa*.

In a single thought-moment of an ordinary person, there are ninety *kṣaṇas*; in one *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing. One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tat-kṣaṇa*; sixty *tat-kṣaṇas* make one *lava*; thirty *lavas* make one *muhūrta*; and thirty *muhūrtas* make one day and night."
This concludes the first explanation regarding the provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the second explanation concerning the inconceivable (*acintya*): at the time when the realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable, one *kalpa* is subsumed within a single *kṣaṇa*, and in a single moment, they universally respond to beings without any distinction; therefore, it is called "one time."
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"There are sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world; for them, the Bodhisattva manifests seven days as one kalpa.
There are sentient beings who do not delight in dwelling long; for them, the Bodhisattva contracts one kalpa into seven days."

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū preached the Lotus Sūtra, those in the assembly who listened did not rise from their seats for sixty intermediate kalpas, yet it was as if they had been sitting for only a meal’s time.
This concludes the second explanation of the time of the inconceivable.

Regarding the third, the correct interpretation of that time: it refers to the day when the Dharma King inaugurated his mission and the occasion when the great assembly gathered in auspicious confluence; therefore, it is called "at one time" (ekasmin samaye).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"When a single sūtra is being taught, from the initial moment of its continuous succession until its ultimate conclusion, it is collectively designated as 'one time.'"
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha explains:

"When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, the seven treasures appear simultaneously; when a Dharma-King appears in the world, the Dharma-treasures appear simultaneously. Because the capacity of the disciples and the teaching are made to coincide without any discrepancy in time, it is called 'at one time' (ekasmin samaye)."
It is said that while the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* establishes the existence of such [distinctions], the Mahāyāna fundamentally has neither coming nor going.
In the age of the eternally manifest and eternal, one falsely perceives empty flowers;
at the beginning of true non-extinction, the kalpa-stone stands here.
To provisionally cite the reason for this: sixty minor kalpas are subsumed within a single moment; it is clearly understood that these are words established through falsehood.
When one relies upon conditions to designate time, the meaning of "time" is such that there is no duality between the speaker and the listener.
Therefore, it is said to be "at one time.
Furthermore, the explanation in the Tripiṭaka states:
"It is named 'one time' because it is complete with ten meanings:"
First, the time when a Buddha appears in the world;
second, the time when the True Dharma is taught;
third, the time when the True Dharma is heard.
4. The time of upholding the true Dharma;
5. The time of reflecting on the true Dharma;
6. The time of practicing the true Dharma.
7. The time of planting the seeds of lower goodness;
8. The time of maturing the seeds of goodness;
9. The time of liberating the seeds of goodness.
Tenth, the time when the mind is impartial.

First, regarding the time when a Buddha appears in the world: just as when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) appears in the world, the seven treasures can be obtained all at once, so too when a Dharma-King appears in the world, the treasure of the Dharma can be heard all at once; those who have not seen [the Buddha] when a Wheel-Turning King appears are enabled to hear [of him].
2. Regarding the time when the True Dharma is preached: when the Buddha preaches the True Dharma, all who are deranged or deaf become awakened; therefore, it is called "one time. 3.
Regarding the time when the True Dharma is heard, there are four causes and conditions:
first, the existence of past causes.
2. Possessing right faith;
3. aspiring with joy;
4. generating respect.
Because these causes and conditions are present at the time of listening to the Dharma, it is called "at one time.
Fourth, regarding the time for upholding the True Dharma, there are three causes and conditions:
first, for the sake of fulfilling one's own practice;
Second, the accomplishment of practice for the sake of others;
third, being a source for others to consult and rely upon.
Possessing these three conditions constitutes the time for upholding the True Dharma.
Fifth, when contemplating the true Dharma, there are five causes and conditions:
first, to contemplate and discern the similar in order to select the true;
second, to contemplate and discern the increasingly superior, like refining pure gold.

Third, the attainment of the fruit through discernment is like the moon becoming bright when clouds are cleared, which all delight in beholding; it is also like a woman’s natural beauty being enhanced by adornments.
Fourth, the inexhaustibility of discernment is like a wish-fulfilling jewel from which wealth emerges without end; likewise, the discernment of phenomena is the inexhaustible manifestation of truth.
Fifth, the benefit of discernment is like seeing the sun’s light at work without ceasing; having attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma, one transforms and guides beings boundlessly.
When these five conditions are present, it is the time for analytical investigation.
Sixth, regarding the time for practicing the true Dharma, there are five causes and conditions:
first, the faculty of wisdom is sharp, thereby eliminating the hindrance of afflictions;
2. Fulfillment of faith eliminates the obstacle of karma;
3. Birth among humans and devas eliminates the obstacle of retribution;
4. Delight in tranquility eliminates the obstacle of distraction.
Fifth, encountering the Buddha’s True Dharma and eliminating obstacles by turning away from evil.
Possessing these five conditions constitutes the opportune time for excellent cultivation.
Seventh, regarding the time for planting the seeds of lower goodness: there are ten causes for the arousal of the bodhicitta.
First, based on the fundamental, because of the Buddha-nature;
second, based on the vessel, by relying on the paths of humans and devas;
third, based on the stages, by relying on the eight dhyānas.
4. Relying on the Three Jewels, for the sake of non-retrogression in practice;
5. Relying on causes, by taking all sentient beings as the cause for planting seeds;
6. Relying on the aspiration of intention, by generating only the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
7. Based on wisdom, because one contemplates faults and virtues;
8. Based on faith, because one has faith in the Three Jewels, the Four Truths, and the seven points;
9. Based on practice, because one relies on practices such as cutting off one's own flesh to feed a hawk.
Tenth, regarding dedication: all roots of goodness are dedicated for the sake of sentient beings.
When these ten matters are present, it is termed the "time of planting inferior seeds.
Eighth, regarding the time of accomplishing the seeds of goodness, there are four causes and conditions:
First, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, which is the perfection of causes;
second, being born in a central land, which is the correspondence of place;
third, drawing near to virtuous friends and receiving their instruction for the sake of others.
Fourth, practicing according to the teachings and remaining free from all negligence.
When these four conditions are present, it is called the time of accomplishing the seeds of goodness.
Ninth, regarding the time of liberating the seeds of goodness, there are five causal conditions:
First, the time of associating with virtuous friends;
second, the time of hearing the true Dharma;
third, the time of upholding the true Dharma.
Fourth, the time for contemplating the True Dharma;
fifth, the time for taking refuge in the True Dharma.
Possessing these five conditions is called the time for the seeds of liberation.

Tenth, regarding the time when the mind is equanimous: if the mind is uneven—either haughty or dejected—one cannot enter into the hearing of the Dharma. If one can uproot both sunkenness and agitation so that mindfulness and wisdom are equal, one attains entry into the True Dharma; this is called the time when the mind is equanimous.
"Because it possesses these ten meanings, it is called 'at one time' (ekasmin samaye).
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Dīrghaśrotra explained "time" as follows:
"There are three kinds:"
First, the period of temporal division;
second, the inconceivable period;
third, the period of provisional designation.

First, regarding the time of segmented [existence]: its substance consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and its characteristics consist of the four phases (*catasraḥ lakṣaṇāni*). It is the limit of retribution for a single lifetime, like a potter’s wheel; when the worldly limit is reached, it ceases. This is called the time of the segmented body.

Second, regarding the inconceivable period of transformation and change: this refers to the continuous succession of birth-and-death through transformation and change, which is difficult to know in terms of its limits within the dharmas; thus it is called the inconceivable period of transformation and change.
Third, regarding conventional designations for time: in foreign lands it is called *kalpa*, which itself has three meanings:
first, *kāla*; second, *samaya*.
Third, worldly renown. "Kāla" (迦羅) here means "distinctive characteristic.

For example, regarding the formulation of the precepts: one hears of the major precepts at the time they are established for the major precepts, but does not hear of them at the time of the minor precepts; one hears of them when one is a monastic, but does not hear of them when one is a layperson; and a king may hear of them, whereas others do not.

Second, regarding the *samaya* time: this is translated as "the time for destroying false views. For the five sections of the Āgamas and the ninefold Dharma, it may be employed by anyone, regardless of whether they are of the "black" or "white" classes.

Third, regarding "at one time" (ekasmin samaye): for example, it is said that at one time [the Buddha] was in the Madhyama-vana grove, and at another time on the banks of the Ganges. Such expressions as "modulating the voice" and "arising and turning" are the conventional linguistic usages of worldly people. Because they cause one to rely upon [the teachings] when refuting wrong views and because they correspond to worldly convention, it is called "at one time."
Question:
"Upon what basis is 'time' established herein? Answer:
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Time is a conceptual image of temporal stages (avasthā) provisionally established upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Because it is established collectively based on form, mind, and so forth, it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*)."
The three preceding variations collectively conclude the explanation of the third period of accomplishment.
Regarding the term "Bhagavān" (the Blessed One),
the commentary states:
The fourth is the primary accomplishment.
This is also analyzed through three sections:
first, the explanation of the name Bhagavān;
The second explains the body of the Bhagavat;
the third explains the term "Supreme Lord" (Īśvara).
Regarding the first explanation of the name Bhagavat, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"He possesses great power and is able to destroy the Great Māra; therefore, he is called Bhagavān.
It is also said:
"Sitting serenely and peacefully upon the seat of enlightenment, he effortlessly subdues Māra; because he possesses such great power, he is called Bhagavān."
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is said:
"The term Bhagavat possesses six meanings;
the first is sovereignty (*vaśitā*)."
The second is Blazing Brilliance;
the third is Majestic Dignity;
the fourth is Renown.
The fifth is auspiciousness;
the sixth is the meaning of nobility.
Regarding the first meaning, sovereignty: it is called sovereignty because one is not struck down or bound by any afflictions.
The second meaning, "blazing," is because it is refined by the fierce flames of the fire of wisdom.
The third meaning, "majestic," is because it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The fourth meaning of "name" (nāma) is that all supreme qualities are completely perfected.
The fifth meaning of "auspiciousness" (śrī) is that humans and devas draw near to offer worship.
The sixth meaning of "Noble" (Bhagavat) is that he brings about the peace and happiness of sentient beings by endowing them with all virtuous qualities.
One who possesses these six meanings is called Bhagavat.
Regarding the "four māras": first is the *skandha-māra*, which has the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its essence.
Second, the destruction of the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), which has as its essence the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);

third, the destruction of the māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*), which consists of the five out-flowing aggregates (*pañca skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ*), meaning that their characteristic of impermanence is termed the māra of death.
Fourth, he destroys the celestial Māras; for the sixth [class], the devaputras of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, constitute the celestial Māras.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* (Sapoduo lun) states:
"Because he is able to destroy the four kinds of Māras, he is named Bhagavat."
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Beneath the Bodhi tree, he destroyed all affliction-māras; upon the Vajra-seat, he destroyed all celestial-māras; by extending his life for three months, he destroyed all death-māras; and by entering nirvāṇa, he destroyed all aggregate-māras."
Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* briefly explains the meaning of destroying the Māras:

"By contemplating emptiness, one destroys the aggregate-māra; by contemplating signlessness, one destroys the affliction-māra; by contemplating wishlessness, one destroys the death-māra; and by possessing the three types of dedication toward bodhi, one destroys the celestial-māra."
It is further said:

"First, by contemplating the impurity of the body, one destroys the Māra of the aggregates; second, by contemplating that sensation is suffering, one destroys the Māra of afflictions; third, by contemplating that the body is impermanent, one destroys the Māra of death; fourth, by contemplating that phenomena are selfless, one destroys the Māra of devas."
"Endowed with these six meanings, one is named Bhagavān.
This is the first explanation of the name Bhagavān.
Second, regarding the explanation of the body of the Bhagavān, there are three meanings:
First, the reward body (saṃbhogakāya);
second, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);
third, the dharma body (dharmakāya).
The first is the *saṃbhogakāya*, which preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The second is the *nirmāṇakāya*, which preaches the Dharma for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
The third is the *dharmakāya*, which is eternally quiescent, benefiting both oneself and others.

Although there are three distinct aspects, the vision is not different. The difference is like that of a śrāvaka seeing a body sixteen feet tall, a bodhisattva seeing an infinite body, and a Buddha seeing the dharma-nature body; likewise, from a single rope, three appearances arise: to one with cataracts it appears as a snake, to one with clear vision it appears as a rope, and to a wise person who examines it closely, only the hemp is seen. The retributive, transformational, and dharma bodies are also like this.
If they are considered in their totality, then the three are one, and the one is the three.

If they are described individually, then the three are not three, and the one is not one. It is like water, ice, and waves—which, though distinct in these three forms, are such that the water is the ice and the water is the water; there are no waves apart from water, and no water apart from waves. The Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya are also like this.
This concludes the second explanation of the body of the Bhagavān.
Regarding the third [explanation], the correct interpretation of the principal term [Bhagavān], according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it states:
"There are five kinds:..."
First, that spoken by the Buddha;
second, that spoken by the noble disciples;
third, that spoken by the devas.
"Fourth is the discourse of celestial immortals;
fifth is the discourse on transformations.
Now it is clarified that this sutra is precisely the teaching of the Buddha, for the Buddha is the Master of the Teaching.
Regarding the term "Buddha," its meaning is "awakening," which is of three kinds:
first, self-awakening; second, awakening others;
[and third, awakening all beings].
Third is the fulfillment of awakening.
Śrāvakas are able to awaken for themselves alone by attaining the wisdom of the emptiness of persons;
although Bodhisattvas attain the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, their awakening is not yet fulfilled.
The Buddhas have realized themselves and awakened others, and their practice of awakening is perfected; thus they are called Buddhas.

A Buddha is the Dharma King of the triple world and the compassionate father of the four modes of birth. He radiates divine light across a thousand lands and showers the rain of Dharma upon the five burning realms. Therefore, non-Buddhists take refuge in him and celestial Māras bow their heads in homage. His jade-like brow-hair is so pure that it illuminates the hells until they vanish; his cranial protuberance is so lofty that gods and humans cannot perceive its limit. Because he is difficult to understand and difficult to fathom, he is titled "Buddha."
Although there have been three different types [of explanations] above, this concludes the general explanation of the fourth point: the accomplishment of the master of the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "residing in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park":
The commentary states:
This is the accomplishment of the fifth station.
It also has three types:
The first reveals the country;
the second reveals the forest;
the third reveals the garden.

First, as for the manifestation of the country, it is the kingdom of Śrāvastī; in the language of Han, it is called the City of Renown (Míngwén Chéng). Because its eminent sages and great scholars of vast learning possess a glorious reputation that resounds afar, it is thus named the City of Renown.

Formerly called Śrāvastī, this is the kingdom of Madhyadeśa in Central India; it was the city ruled by King Prasenajit during the Buddha’s lifetime, with a circumference of over six thousand *li*. Within the city are two *stūpas*:
one is the vihāra of the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, and the other is the *stūpa* within the former residence of the elder Sudatta.
This concludes the first section, which clarifies the country.
Second, as for clarifying the grove: this refers to his dwelling in the Jeta Grove. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, he dwelt in the Jeta Grove."
Regarding the term "abiding," it refers to one of the four modes of deportment.
There are three kinds of abiding:
